'''Frances Hardcastle''' (13 August 1866 – 26 December 1941) was an English mathematician, in 1894 one of the founding members of the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref name="Kenschaft2005">{{cite book|first=Patricia C.|last= Kenschaft|authorlink=Patricia Clark Kenschaft|title=Change Is Possible: Stories of Women And Minorities in Mathematics|url=https://archive.org/details/changeispossible0000kens|url-access=registration|year=2005|publisher=American Mathematical Society|isbn=978-0-8218-3748-1|page=[https://archive.org/details/changeispossible0000kens/page/47 47]}}</ref> Her work included contributions to the theory of [[point group]]s.<ref name="Ogilvie2000" />

== Biography ==
Born in Writtle, just outside [[Chelmsford]], [[Essex]],<ref name="Ogilvie2000" /><ref>"Hardcastle, Frances / Chelmsford 4a 162" in ''General Index to Births in England and Wales'' (1866)</ref> Hardcastle was a daughter of Henry Hardcastle, a barrister,<ref name="CreeseCreese1998">{{cite book|last1=Creese|first1=Mary R.S. |last2=Creese|first2=Thomas M.|title=Ladies in the Laboratory? American and British Women in Science, 1800-1900: A Survey of Their Contributions to Research|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=amtGAwAAQBAJ&pg=PA195|year=1998|publisher=Scarecrow Press|isbn=978-0-585-27684-7|pages=195–}}</ref> by his marriage in 1865 to Maria Sophia Herschel,<ref>"Herschel, Maria Sophia, Hardcastle, Henry / Cranbrook	 2a 1041" in ''General Index to Marriages in England and Wales'' (1865)</ref> daughter of the astronomer, mathematician, and chemist [[John Herschel|Sir John Herschel]].<ref name="Ogilvie2000">{{cite book|first1=M. |last1=Ogilvie|first2=Joy|last2=Harvey|author-link=Marilyn Bailey Ogilvie|author2-link=Joy Harvey|title=The Biographical Dictionary of Women in Science: Pioneering Lives From Ancient Times to the Mid-20th Century|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QmfyK0QtsRAC&pg=PA555|date= 2000|publisher=Taylor & Francis US|isbn=978-0-415-92038-4|page=555}}</ref>

She was educated at [[Girton College, Cambridge|Girton College]] (Tripos Part I 1891 & Part II 1892), and obtained a Certificate in Mathematics.<ref name="Ogilvie2000" /><ref name="Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society">{{cite book|title=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PljxAAAAMAAJ|access-date=19 October 2012|year=1942|publisher=Society}}</ref>

In 1892, she went to the [[University of Chicago]] for a year as an honorary fellow, then spent another year at [[Bryn Mawr College]] studying under [[Charlotte Scott]].  While at Bryn Mawr she was president of the Graduate Club and translated [[Felix Klein]]'s book ''On Riemann's Theory of Algebraic functions and Integrals''.  In 1895, she recommenced postgraduate studies at Cambridge, and within a few years had published several papers on point-groups.  She earned a BA degree from the University of London in 1903.<ref name="Ogilvie2000" /> [[Trinity College Dublin]] awarded her an [[Master of Arts (Oxford, Cambridge, and Dublin)|MA]] ([[ad eundem degree|ad eundem]]) in 1905.

Hardcastle was one of 156 British women who publicly supported the aims of the [[International Congress of Women#The Hague.2C April. E2.80.93May 1915|International Congress of Women]], held in [[The Hague]] in April 1915. These aims were, "1. To demand that international disputes shall in future be settled by some other means than war," and "2. To claim that women shall have a voice in the affairs of nations."<ref name="Oldfield1994">{{cite book|last=Oldfield|first=Sybil|title=This Working-Day World: Women's Lives And Culture(s) In Britain, 1914–1945|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=p8estpxUIqMC&pg=PA92|date= 1994|publisher=Taylor & Francis|isbn=978-0-7484-0107-9|pages=92–94|chapter=England's Cassandras in World War One}}</ref>
Until 1909, she was an Honorary Secretary of the [[National Union of Women's Suffrage Societies]] (NUWSS).<ref name="Crawford2001">{{cite book|first=Elizab|last= Crawford|title=Women's Suffrage Movement: A Reference Guide, 1866-1928|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eIzLissZmscC&pg=PA442|date= 2001|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-0-415-23926-4|pages=436–442|chapter=National Union of Women's Suffrage Societies}}</ref>

Hardcastle was the lifelong companion of [[Ethel Williams (physician)|Dr Ethel Williams]], a physician, [[Justice of the Peace]], feminist, and social reformer.<ref name="Oldfield2001">{{cite book|last=Oldfield|first=Sybil|title=Women humanitarians: a biographical dictionary of British women active between 1900 and 1950 : 'doers of the word'|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fDUqAAAAYAAJ|date=2001|publisher=Continuum|isbn=978-0-8264-4962-7|pages=276–278}}</ref> She died at the Royal Hotel, Cambridge, on 26 December 1941, when her home address was stated as Low Bridges, [[Stocksfield]], [[Northumberland]], and left a substantial estate valued at £4,400. Probate was granted to Ethel Williams and Mabel Annie Burnip.<ref name=Probate>''Calendar of Grants of Probate in England and Wales'' (1942), [https://probatesearch.service.gov.uk/Calendar?surname=Hardcastle&yearOfDeath=1942&page=1#calendar p. 74], probatesearch.service.gov.uk, accessed 18 October 2020</ref>
